Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on what I have done wrong
never allow myself to feel or express anger
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette: Sang is a 27-year-old South Eastern Asian male who works as a journalist. He has been in a relationship with his partner for several years but recently experienced severe physical abuse at her hands. This traumatic event continues to shape his daily life and emotions, driving him to seek psychological help. The night of the attack was a turning point. Sang had come home late from an assignment and found his partner waiting for him in a rage. She accused him of infidelity, which he vehemently denied but ultimately could not convince her otherwise. The physical abuse followed, leaving Sang with both emotional scars and lingering physical pain. Since then, specific triggers have become potent reminders of the trauma. Riding public transport, particularly buses, has become unbearable due to his fear of being alone in confined spaces with potential threats. Any male presence can also trigger intense anxiety, as he is constantly vigilant for signs of danger from men who might resemble his abusive partner. These triggers are deeply intertwined with his maladaptive coping strategies and intrusive memories. When Sang encounters these triggers, he spirals into self-blame rumination, believing that the abuse was somehow his fault. He dwells on every mistake he has made in his relationship, convinced that there must have been a way to prevent the attack if only he had acted differently. This constant self-criticism is compounded by his tendency to suppress anger. Instead of expressing his feelings, Sang channels them into restrictive eating habits as a form of punishment and control. The memory of the abuse often feels like it’s happening right now rather than something in the past, making him experience overwhelming emotional distress whenever it resurfaces. The physical pain he felt during the attack reoccurs, intensifying his sense of vulnerability. These memories are not just intrusive; they reinforce his negative appraisals about himself and others. Sang's fear that harm can come from anyone at any moment is deeply ingrained in his psyche. He cannot trust assurances of safety, even from those close to him. This mistrust fuels a constant state of alertness and hypervigilance. His nights are plagued by waking up multiple times to check if he is safe, further exacerbating his sense of inadequacy. Sang’s negative appraisals not only feed into his heightened threat perception but also amplify the potency of his triggers. The belief that people can’t be trusted and that he himself is inadequate has led him to isolate himself from others and avoid situations where he might encounter potential threats. His mistrust and fear are reinforced by every instance where something takes longer than expected, leading him to assume the worst. Over time, these maladaptive strategies have taken a toll on Sang’s work as a journalist. He avoids assignments that require public transport or working in environments with male colleagues. His undereating has affected his physical health and energy levels, making it harder for him to focus on his reporting tasks. What finally brought Sang to seek help was the realization that he could no longer function at work and maintain his relationships without support. He is most afraid of never feeling safe again and being trapped in a cycle of fear and mistrust. However, he is also hopeful that therapy can provide him with tools to manage his symptoms and regain control over his life. The traumatic event continues to shape Sang’s experience of the world, but by understanding the interconnectedness of his triggers, memories, negative appraisals, threat perception, and coping strategies, there is a path toward recovery.
